chapter: Los Angeles scene in the 1930s and 40s
title: Early women singers: Roberta Hyson, Lottie Gozier and the Breakfast Club singers
summary: She names Roberta Hyson, Lottie Gozier, Ruth Lee, Betty Treadwell and others, intimate table-to-table singers who died young.

story.theme_name: Going west: California and the Los Angeles scene
story.community_name: Going west: moving to and working in California

blocks.x: You were mentioning today, when you first arrived, about two women performers here, one a lady who worked with the Spikes Brothers Orchestra. What was her name?

Her name was Roberta Hyson. Roberta from what I understand, from what she told me, was one of the first black women to record, in Los Angeles. And there was some connection with the Reb Spikes group. Reb Spikes and
his brother were music writers or music publishers or something, and seemingly there was some connection there with them. I --

She was a singer. A very -- I worked with her, but also we worked at little jobs, a long time ago, the three of us. And incidentally, Sam McDaniels worked with us. He was also very popular when I first came here. Hattie McDaniels' brother. He was a drummer and a terrific entertainer. He had a terrific following.

But there was another woman also. In fact there were two other women. One of them has gone on. Her name was Lottie Gozier. Well, Lottie was a marvelous pianist, and she and Roberta and another woman named Ruth Lee, they tell me they worked together, and I think they recorded. I think the three of them -- Roberta recorded alone, but I think the three of them made records together or something, and they were very, very popular. Now this, of course, must have been around the early '30s, the very early '30s, before I came here. But I did get to meet them, as I say. I worked with Roberta, because at that time, when I first came here, every group had a vocalist, you know. Well, I wasn't singing at that time. I would maybe do one or two songs a night, but I really did not consider myself -- I still didn't, you know, go out as a vocalist, but I did sing a few songs. But each group, little trio, or sometimes just a piano player, would have a vocalist with them.
Would you call these ladies jazz singers?

Well, I guess you would call them that. No, they weren't just jazz singers. Some of them were -- at that time it was a thing where they used to go to the tables, you know. They used to have -- the clubs were all, naturally, intimate spots, and they would go around to the various tables. Now, they'd work with a piano player and they'd go around to the tables and sing intimate songs. So I don't think this would be so much called jazz, for all of these people that I've talked about. But this is what people wanted, they wanted to hear.

Some of them -- another singer that comes to mind was Betty Treadwell. I think I mentioned Betty. She was one of the singers from the Breakfast Club, over the Club Alabam. And these singers worked, they did pop and some of them did a little dancing. Anita Brown, who was a very beautiful girl, and she was very popular, and another girl was Billie Brown, and another one was Bonnie Bryant. Well, these women were all entertainers that could sing and dance, you know, and every little spot, as I say, featured entertainment. Every spot, I don't care where you went, what section of the town you would go in, you know, even on Central Avenue. There was entertainment.
Oh, there was lots of entertainment there.
Yeah, an awful lot of entertainment. Everywhere you went you'd be entertained, you know. So I'm

very glad that I came along at that time, because I got to see these people, because most of these people are gone that I'm talking about now, and they weren't that old. Anita Brown was certainly not very old when she died. Bonnie Bryant was not that old. Billie Brown was not that old. It's amazing how they died so very young, all of these women that I'm talking about. They were very young women.
